solutions.text: PHẦN A

1. Only the most capable students get promoted in an educational meritocracy. Ghi chú: "Meritocracy" là danh từ trừu tượng chỉ hệ thống dựa trên năng lực; tránh viết "a meritocracy system" vì thừa từ. Collocation thường gặp: "a functioning meritocracy", "an educational meritocracy".

2. Rote learning does not help students think for themselves. Ghi chú: "Rote learning" (học vẹt) luôn đi cùng "learning", không tách rời thành "rote" đứng một mình khi làm chủ ngữ. Đối lập với "holistic learning".

3. Many families in the countryside cannot afford tertiary education for their children. Ghi chú: "Tertiary" nghĩa là bậc ba (sau "primary" và "secondary"), dễ nhầm với "territory". Đồng nghĩa trang trọng: "higher education".

4. Submitting another student's essay as your own is a serious case of plagiarism. Ghi chú: "Plagiarism" là danh từ không đếm được; động từ tương ứng là "plagiarise" (Anh) chứ không phải "plagiarism" ở dạng động từ.

5. The school introduced stricter rules after noticing rising truancy among certain students. Ghi chú: "Truancy" là hành vi trừu tượng (sự trốn học); người trốn học gọi là "a truant", không phải "a truancy".

6. The fees at some private universities are exorbitant for an average family. Ghi chú: "Exorbitant" chỉ dùng cho giá cả, phí, hoặc yêu cầu — không dùng để mô tả kích thước vật lý. Đồng nghĩa: "extortionate".

7. The pedagogy used to train teachers has changed a great deal over the past decade. Ghi chú: Trong tiếng Anh-Anh, đuôi "-gogy" phát âm nhẹ /-dʒi/, không đọc nặng như kiểu Mỹ. "Pedagogy" là phương pháp/lý luận giảng dạy, khác "pedagogue" (người dạy học, thường mang sắc thái cổ hủ).

8. The curriculum is set by the Ministry of Education. Ghi chú: Số nhiều học thuật là "curricula"; tránh dùng "curriculums" trong văn phong academic. Phân biệt với "syllabus" (đề cương một môn học cụ thể).

9. From a young age, she showed a clear natural aptitude for mathematics. Ghi chú: "Aptitude" (năng khiếu bẩm sinh) dễ viết nhầm thành "attitude" (thái độ) vì gần giống mặt chữ. Collocation: "an aptitude test", "aptitude for a subject".

10. Extracurricular clubs and sports teams give students a break from academic pressure. Ghi chú: Viết liền thành một từ "extracurricular", không tách thành "extra curricular". Từ gốc: "curriculum" + "curricular" (adj).
11. Governments often see spending on schools as an investment in human capital. Ghi chú: "Human capital" là thuật ngữ kinh tế học, không viết hoa, không có số nhiều ("human capitals" là sai).

12. He did not study very hard, but he still managed to scrape through the final exam. Ghi chú: "Scrape through" hàm ý đậu một cách chật vật, sát nút — trái nghĩa với "pass with flying colours" (đậu xuất sắc).
PHẦN B

1. Band 7: Self-taught individuals often acquire impressive skills without any formal instruction. Band 8: Were the world's great autodidacts judged solely by their credentials, many of history's most original minds would never have been recognised. (Were + S + to-V inversion)

2. Band 7: Schools ought to nurture students' holistic development rather than focusing narrowly on grades. Band 8: What contemporary pedagogy increasingly champions is a holistic framework, one privileging emotional intelligence and creativity over narrow academic metrics. (cleft + nominalisation)

3. Band 7: Vocational training can be just as valuable as a university degree. Band 8: Not only does vocational training furnish students with immediately marketable skills, but it also dismantles the outdated snobbery that still surrounds technical trades. (negative inversion)

4. Band 7: Asynchronous online courses allow students to study at a time that suits them. Band 8: It is the asynchronous nature of online learning — rather than its content — that constitutes its single greatest advantage over the traditional lecture hall. (cleft sentence)

5. Band 7: Reputable schools maintain a rigorous curriculum and set high expectations for their students. Band 8: So rigorous have the academic standards at these institutions become that mediocrity is, quite simply, not tolerated. (so + adj inversion)

6. Band 7: Once errors become habitual, they are notoriously difficult to correct. Band 8: What linguists term fossilisation sets in once errors become habituated, rendering them extraordinarily resistant to correction even with targeted intervention. (cleft + reduced relative)

7. Band 7: Not all students are given an equal opportunity to succeed academically. Band 8: Rarely is a genuinely level playing field afforded to students from disadvantaged backgrounds, however meritocratic the system purports to be. (negative inversion)

8. Band 7: Being an avid reader from an early age set her apart from her peers. Band 8: Branded something of a bookworm throughout her childhood, she nonetheless credits her insatiable appetite for books with shaping her intellectual trajectory. (reduced relative)

passages.text: Few ideas in contemporary educational research have travelled as far, or as unevenly, as metacognition. The term, coined by the developmental psychologist John Flavell at Stanford in 1976, refers to the capacity to monitor and regulate one's own cognitive processes — to know, as Flavell put it, "what one knows, and what one does not". Within three decades it had become a near-mandatory category in school-improvement frameworks across the United Kingdom, Australia and the Netherlands. The Education Endowment Foundation, an influential English charity that ranks classroom interventions by cost-effectiveness, has repeatedly placed "metacognition and self-regulation" among its top three recommended strategies, with a headline figure of "seven months of additional progress" per pupil per year. Yet a closer reading of the underlying research reveals a body of evidence whose internal disagreements have rarely reached the wider audience.

The case for metacognitive instruction rests on a series of well-replicated laboratory findings. Students explicitly taught to plan, monitor and evaluate their problem-solving steps tend to outperform peers who receive identical content without the metacognitive scaffolding. Professor Marcel Veenman of Leiden University, whose laboratory has run controlled studies since the 1990s, reports an average effect size that, by educational standards, is unusually robust. Veenman argues that metacognitive skill is a partly domain-general capacity: a student trained to reflect on her mathematical reasoning will generalise some of that habit to history essays and laboratory reports, although the transfer is rarely complete. The mechanism, he proposes, lies in the slowing of automatic processing long enough for working memory to allocate attention deliberately.

A second, related strand has emerged from research on cognitive load. Professor John Sweller, an Australian educational psychologist whose framework dates to the late 1980s, has long maintained that human working memory is severely limited and that effective instruction must respect this constraint. Sweller and his collaborators have warned that metacognitive prompts, if poorly designed, may themselves consume scarce cognitive resources, producing what they term "metacognitive load". Far from accelerating learning, such poorly timed interventions may displace the very rehearsal needed to consolidate new material. The implication is uncomfortable for enthusiasts: the same instructional move that produces gains in one experimental condition may produce losses in another, depending on the learner's prior knowledge and the structural complexity of the task.

The first sustained challenge to the metacognitive consensus appeared around 2018, when a research team led by Dr Robert de Bruin at the University of Maastricht reviewed seventy-three classroom trials and reported that the average effect, once unpublished studies were included, was less than half the figure quoted in policy summaries. De Bruin attributed the gap partly to publication bias — researchers who found null results were under-represented in the literature — and partly to inconsistent definitions: what counts as a "metacognitive intervention" varies so widely across studies that aggregating them may be statistically inappropriate. A 2021 meta-analysis by Donker and her colleagues at Groningen broadly confirmed this picture, finding meaningful gains in upper-primary mathematics and reading but very small or null effects in early-years contexts and in vocational training.

Veenman and his supporters have accepted some criticisms while pushing back on others. They concede that not every classroom application has been well designed, and that small-group reflective dialogue is unlikely to transform attainment on its own. They argue, however, that lumping together superficial "thinking-skills" lessons with carefully sequenced metacognitive coaching obscures the picture, because the two interventions differ both in duration and in specificity. The distinction matters, in their view, because the original Flavell programme was always about iterative, task-embedded reflection rather than the brief discussion of "how I learned" common in school assemblies. Critics have replied that this clarification narrows the claim to a subgroup of programmes so specific that the broad public message should be retired or heavily qualified.

A separate and arguably more interesting strand of research has shifted the question from monitoring to motivation. Researchers in educational psychology, including Professor Bonny Daniels at the University of Auckland, have argued that the more reliable effect of metacognitive instruction may not be on cognition narrowly understood but on a learner's developing sense of agency. In repeated interviews, secondary-school pupils who have completed structured reflection programmes describe themselves as more willing to attempt difficult problems, more comfortable with productive failure, and more inclined to seek feedback. Such effects are difficult to capture in short-term reaction-time tasks but appear with reasonable consistency in qualitative studies across continents. The implication, in Daniels's view, is that the durable benefit of metacognition lies in the disposition it cultivates rather than in any narrow cognitive trick.

What follows for policy is considerable. Should the chief value of metacognitive teaching lie in fostering self-direction rather than in lifting raw test scores, the conversations most worth having will turn on how classrooms allocate time for reflection, how teachers model their own uncertainty, and how examinations reward the disposition to revise. The argument, in the writer's view, merits closer examination than it has so far drawn, partly because it is less amenable to commercial exploitation than the headline effect-size figures.

None of this settles the underlying cognitive debate. Neuroimaging carried out at the Donders Institute in Nijmegen has detected heightened activity in the prefrontal regions tied to self-monitoring whenever learners are asked to reflect on their own thinking, yet the gap between such signatures and durable classroom gains remains wide. The honest conclusion is therefore a qualified one. Metacognitive instruction is no universal accelerator, despite the confidence of policy summaries; equally, it is far more than a passing fashion. Its real contribution may lie less in raising test scores than in subtly reshaping the relationship between learners and their own effort — an effect that is easy to feel in a classroom but stubbornly hard to quantify.

audio_scripts.text: Okay, settle down. Today's supervision — Theo and Jasmine on play-based learning in early-years settings. Theo, you wanna start? And for the recording, surname spelling please.
Yeah. So I'm Theo Kowalczyk — that's K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K, the C-Z makes a "ch" sound. My fieldwork was at Brackenfield Nursery, observing thirty-six children aged four to five. (Q1)

Erm, the observation phase started in October 2023 — sorry, no, September 2023, October was when I began coding the video data. The intervention itself ran for eight weeks and concluded in December. (Q2)

Right. And just to anchor the timeframe for the recording — your data USED TO be analysed in NVivo, you've NOW migrated to MAXQDA, and from next year you'LL be piloting an AI-assisted coding pipeline, correct?

Well, the dominant framework here is what Kathy Sylva termed "sustained shared thinking". And, you know, the terminology in this literature is genuinely overlapping — you'll encounter labels like collaborative inquiry, joint reasoning, co-constructed cognition, all referring to broadly the same pedagogical exchange. The currently accepted scholarly term, however, is sustained shared thinking. I've used that throughout. (Q3)

Yeah, and I'm gonna build on Theo's framing. In my parallel sample — forty-five Reception-year pupils across two Manchester schools — most of the teachers said they incorporate guided play AT LEAST four times a day. Actually, sorry, let me be precise — thirty-one out of forty-five, which is about sixty-nine per cent. Only a few — roughly twelve per cent — restricted play to designated slots, and some — nineteen per cent — used it intermittently. (Q4)
Mm. Theo, did your data corroborate the "play improves literacy outcomes" thesis?

Sorta, yeah, with significant qualifiers. Most of the children I observed did NOT show statistically significant phonological gains from unstructured play alone. The naive assumption — that any play boosts literacy — well, isn't supported. Only when an adult scaffolded the play did we see measurable phoneme-awareness uplift. (Q5)

And, dunno about your cohort, but I noticed something striking on the screen-time substitution axis. So-called digital play — apps that mimic structured tasks — that's actually displacing physical play in higher-income suburbs, not the lower ones, contrary to received wisdom. And the developmental psychology literature warns this restricts a child's gross-motor consolidation.
Interesting. Jasmine, did you stratify by school income band?
Kinda. We binned schools by free-school-meal eligibility. Counter-intuitively, schools with the LOWEST proportion of free-meal pupils reported the MOST screen-mediated play at home, not the highest.
Well, it's about parental device access — affluent parents hand over tablets to buy themselves working time, so paradoxically their kids accumulate more passive screen exposure.

And one final point — peer-interaction data. In single-child households, collaborative play episodes were considerably shorter than in households with siblings. Researchers attribute this to attentional habituation — solo children disengage faster when peers behave unpredictably.

Right. Now, going back to what Theo flagged at the outset — that "currently accepted scholarly term" — that's the construct we'll unpack in next week's seminar. And Jasmine, on your sixty-nine-per-cent figure: the implication that guided play is normative chimes with Sylva, but Theo's literacy caveat tempers it. Useful tension. Thanks both. (Q6)

blocks.text: Whether university education should be made free or continue to require tuition fees is a controversial issue in many countries. This essay will examine both sides of the argument before suggesting that a means-tested system represents the most defensible compromise.

Supporters of tuition-free universities argue that exorbitant fees deter capable students from low-income households, thereby undermining a genuine meritocracy. Countries such as Germany, for example, have abolished tuition for domestic students and still maintain a rigorous academic standard. It is this kind of model that arguably maximises human capital, since no talented young person is excluded from tertiary education simply because of their financial background. Moreover, removing fees could ease the student-debt crisis, which currently delays many graduates from buying houses or starting families.

On the other side, critics contend that providing free higher education places a heavy burden on taxpayers, many of whom never benefit from a degree themselves. There is also a concern that, without the financial commitment of tuition fees, students may take their studies less seriously, leading to higher rates of truancy and procrastination. Furthermore, an unrestricted intake might cause degree devaluation, since employers struggle to distinguish candidates when nearly everyone holds a bachelor's qualification.

In my opinion, neither extreme is fully satisfactory, and the most workable solution lies somewhere in between. Tuition should be heavily subsidised but not entirely waived; students from disadvantaged families ought to receive needs-based scholarships, while those who can comfortably afford fees should contribute. Such a system protects equity without bankrupting the public purse, and a modest contribution would encourage the academic discipline that fully free systems sometimes struggle to maintain.

Whether tertiary education ought to be publicly financed or remain fee-based is a debate that cuts to the heart of contemporary educational policy. While both positions have considerable merit, I shall argue that a calibrated, means-tested model — rather than universal tuition or wholesale gratuity — best reconciles the competing imperatives of access, efficiency and fiscal sustainability.

Advocates of free university maintain that exorbitant tuition entrenches socio-economic stratification. Cross-national data appear to support this: Germany and several Nordic states, having abolished domestic fees, report relatively high participation rates among first-generation students. It is precisely this widening of the educational pipeline that proponents regard as essential to a functioning meritocracy. Were tuition entirely removed, moreover, the chilling effect of debt on consumption and family formation — particularly acute in the United States, where outstanding student liabilities exceed USD 1.7 trillion — would arguably be mitigated.

Opponents, by contrast, contend that universal gratuity is fiscally regressive. Public funds, drawn disproportionately from non-graduate taxpayers, are channelled toward future high earners, a transfer difficult to justify on equity grounds. Not only does indiscriminate provision risk degree devaluation, but it may also weaken academic commitment, since tuition, however modest, often functions as a commitment device against procrastination. By the same token, blanket subsidies tend to crowd out investment in the vocational pathways the labour market increasingly demands.

The position I would advocate, accordingly, is a tiered model contingent upon household income: full subsidy for the lowest quintile, sliding contributions for the middle, and means-tested loans for the affluent. Such an architecture preserves the egalitarian ethos of free access while inoculating the system against the moral hazard and fiscal drift that critics rightly identify. Notwithstanding the political difficulty of implementation, it is calibration — not abolition — that should guide reform.

solutions.text: PHẦN A

1. Only the most capable students get promoted in an educational meritocracy. Ghi chú: "Meritocracy" là danh từ trừu tượng chỉ hệ thống dựa trên năng lực; tránh viết "a meritocracy system" vì thừa từ. Collocation thường gặp: "a functioning meritocracy", "an educational meritocracy".

2. Rote learning does not help students think for themselves. Ghi chú: "Rote learning" (học vẹt) luôn đi cùng "learning", không tách rời thành "rote" đứng một mình khi làm chủ ngữ. Đối lập với "holistic learning".

3. Many families in the countryside cannot afford tertiary education for their children. Ghi chú: "Tertiary" nghĩa là bậc ba (sau "primary" và "secondary"), dễ nhầm với "territory". Đồng nghĩa trang trọng: "higher education".

4. Submitting another student's essay as your own is a serious case of plagiarism. Ghi chú: "Plagiarism" là danh từ không đếm được; động từ tương ứng là "plagiarise" (Anh) chứ không phải "plagiarism" ở dạng động từ.

5. The school introduced stricter rules after noticing rising truancy among certain students. Ghi chú: "Truancy" là hành vi trừu tượng (sự trốn học); người trốn học gọi là "a truant", không phải "a truancy".

6. The fees at some private universities are exorbitant for an average family. Ghi chú: "Exorbitant" chỉ dùng cho giá cả, phí, hoặc yêu cầu — không dùng để mô tả kích thước vật lý. Đồng nghĩa: "extortionate".

7. The pedagogy used to train teachers has changed a great deal over the past decade. Ghi chú: Trong tiếng Anh-Anh, đuôi "-gogy" phát âm nhẹ /-dʒi/, không đọc nặng như kiểu Mỹ. "Pedagogy" là phương pháp/lý luận giảng dạy, khác "pedagogue" (người dạy học, thường mang sắc thái cổ hủ).

8. The curriculum is set by the Ministry of Education. Ghi chú: Số nhiều học thuật là "curricula"; tránh dùng "curriculums" trong văn phong academic. Phân biệt với "syllabus" (đề cương một môn học cụ thể).

9. From a young age, she showed a clear natural aptitude for mathematics. Ghi chú: "Aptitude" (năng khiếu bẩm sinh) dễ viết nhầm thành "attitude" (thái độ) vì gần giống mặt chữ. Collocation: "an aptitude test", "aptitude for a subject".

10. Extracurricular clubs and sports teams give students a break from academic pressure. Ghi chú: Viết liền thành một từ "extracurricular", không tách thành "extra curricular". Từ gốc: "curriculum" + "curricular" (adj).
11. Governments often see spending on schools as an investment in human capital. Ghi chú: "Human capital" là thuật ngữ kinh tế học, không viết hoa, không có số nhiều ("human capitals" là sai).

12. He did not study very hard, but he still managed to scrape through the final exam. Ghi chú: "Scrape through" hàm ý đậu một cách chật vật, sát nút — trái nghĩa với "pass with flying colours" (đậu xuất sắc).
PHẦN B

1. Band 7: Self-taught individuals often acquire impressive skills without any formal instruction. Band 8: Were the world's great autodidacts judged solely by their credentials, many of history's most original minds would never have been recognised. (Were + S + to-V inversion)

2. Band 7: Schools ought to nurture students' holistic development rather than focusing narrowly on grades. Band 8: What contemporary pedagogy increasingly champions is a holistic framework, one privileging emotional intelligence and creativity over narrow academic metrics. (cleft + nominalisation)

3. Band 7: Vocational training can be just as valuable as a university degree. Band 8: Not only does vocational training furnish students with immediately marketable skills, but it also dismantles the outdated snobbery that still surrounds technical trades. (negative inversion)

4. Band 7: Asynchronous online courses allow students to study at a time that suits them. Band 8: It is the asynchronous nature of online learning — rather than its content — that constitutes its single greatest advantage over the traditional lecture hall. (cleft sentence)

5. Band 7: Reputable schools maintain a rigorous curriculum and set high expectations for their students. Band 8: So rigorous have the academic standards at these institutions become that mediocrity is, quite simply, not tolerated. (so + adj inversion)

6. Band 7: Once errors become habitual, they are notoriously difficult to correct. Band 8: What linguists term fossilisation sets in once errors become habituated, rendering them extraordinarily resistant to correction even with targeted intervention. (cleft + reduced relative)

7. Band 7: Not all students are given an equal opportunity to succeed academically. Band 8: Rarely is a genuinely level playing field afforded to students from disadvantaged backgrounds, however meritocratic the system purports to be. (negative inversion)

8. Band 7: Being an avid reader from an early age set her apart from her peers. Band 8: Branded something of a bookworm throughout her childhood, she nonetheless credits her insatiable appetite for books with shaping her intellectual trajectory. (reduced relative)

The Student Debt Crisis: Exorbitant tuition fees are causing a massive student debt crisis globally, making young adults delay buying houses or starting families.
Rise of EdTech & AI: The integration of AI (like ChatGPT) is forcing educators to change how they assess students, moving away from take-home essays to prevent plagiarism.
Degree Inflation: Having a bachelor's degree is no longer a guarantee of a good job; hence, a master's degree (dissertation/thesis) is becoming the new baseline.

2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Free University Education (Should tertiary education be free?)
Arguments FOR (Agree): Promotes an egalitarian society (bình đẳng); maximises human capital by ensuring no talent is wasted due to poverty; creates a highly literate and skilled workforce.

Arguments AGAINST (Disagree): Imposes a massive financial burden on taxpayers; may lead to degree devaluation (bằng cấp mất giá) and overcrowded universities; lack of financial commitment might increase drop-out rates.
Topic: Academic vs. Vocational Education
Academic Pros: Fosters critical thinking, research, and innovation; essential for professions like medicine, law, and academia.
Vocational Pros: Addresses immediate job market needs; provides practical, hands-on skills; often results in quicker employment and less debt.
Topic: Standardised Testing
Pros: Provides an objective, scalable way to measure student performance; creates a baseline for a meritocratic system.
Cons: Encourages rote learning (teaching to the test); causes severe anxiety and peer pressure; ignores holistic development and creative potential.

The course I'd be utterly captivated to enrol in is an MSc in Cognitive Neuroscience, ideally at University College London, whose research output in this field is, by all accounts, world-leading. (hedging)

What initially drew me to this discipline is the elegant way it sits at the crossroads of psychology, biology, and computer science. (cleft) It's essentially the rigorous, evidence-based study of how the brain gives rise to mind — a question philosophers have wrestled with for millennia, but which modern imaging has only recently begun to illuminate.

The programme typically runs for twelve intensive months, comprising taught modules on neuroplasticity, computational modelling, and a substantial dissertation. Were I to secure a place, I'd most likely pursue a doctorate afterwards, since one year barely scratches the surface. (conditional inversion)

Several factors converge to make this pivot so compelling. First, my undergraduate background was in literature, yet what I've discovered over the past two years is an almost obsessive fascination with autodidactic learning and how adults rewire their brains in mid-life — a phenomenon known as adult neuroplasticity. (cleft) Second, not only would the course furnish me with cutting-edge research methodology, but it would also open doors to the burgeoning EdTech sector. (negative inversion)

Driven by mounting curiosity rather than career calculation, I genuinely believe this is the field where I could contribute meaningfully. (reduced relative) The acquisition of this knowledge, frankly, would feel less like work and more like coming home intellectually. (nominalisation)

To borrow an idiom, it would be a chance to hit the books with real purpose (informal idiom) — and arguably pass the threshold with flying colours rather than merely scraping through. (informal idiom)

blocks.text: Q1. Should higher education be more vocational?
P: There is a compelling case for rebalancing higher education towards vocational pathways, particularly in economies plagued by graduate underemployment.
E: As degree inflation erodes the signalling power of bachelor's degrees and skilled-trades shortages mount, the binary between academic and vocational tracks looks increasingly anachronistic.

E: The OECD's Education at a Glance (2023) report found that across member states, 30% of tertiary graduates are working in jobs that don't require a degree — a phenomenon termed "credential mismatch". Conversely, Germany's dual-VET system, which channels roughly half of upper-secondary students into apprenticeships, has yielded youth unemployment of just 6% (Eurostat, 2023), versus 22% in Spain where vocational pathways are stigmatised. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs (2023) further projects 23% labour-market churn by 2027, demanding constant reskilling.
L: Consequently, integrating practical vocational components into tertiary education isn't an abandonment of academia — it's an evolution of it.
Hedging Toolbox: the evidence increasingly points to / by most accounts / not without qualification
Lexical Upgrade Box:
practical training → vocational pathways / hands-on apprenticeships
jobs → labour-market outcomes / employability
useful → economically viable / market-aligned
Sample Answer (94 words):

The evidence increasingly points to higher education becoming more vocationally oriented, though not without qualification. OECD (2023) found 30% of graduates are over-qualified for their roles, while Germany's dual VET model keeps youth unemployment at just 6% versus 22% in Spain (Eurostat, 2023). What developing economies like Vietnam should pursue is a hybrid: maintaining academic rigour while embedding apprenticeships and industry partnerships. Not only does this enhance employability, but it also dismantles the snobbery that still surrounds technical trades — a deeply unhelpful relic of nineteenth-century class hierarchies.
Q2. Is intelligence innate or developed?
P: Intelligence is, by most credible accounts, the product of an intricate interplay between genetic predisposition and environmental enrichment — a textbook nature-nurture entanglement.
E: Heritability studies set the biological floor and ceiling, while education, nutrition, and cognitively stimulating environments determine where within that range one actually lands.

E: The widely cited Minnesota Twin Study (Bouchard et al., 1990) estimated IQ heritability at roughly 50–70%, suggesting a substantial genetic substrate. However, the Flynn Effect — documented across more than 30 countries — shows average IQ scores have risen by approximately 3 points per decade since the 1930s, a shift far too rapid to be genetic and almost certainly attributable to better schooling and nutrition. Furthermore, UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report (2022) correlates early-childhood education investment with measurable gains in cognitive outcomes.
L: Hence, it would be reductive to frame intelligence as either born or made; it's unambiguously both.
Hedging Toolbox: one could plausibly argue / the data lean towards / it would be reductive to suggest
Lexical Upgrade Box:
smart → cognitively endowed / intellectually able
born with → genetically predisposed
learn → acquire / cultivate
Sample Answer (93 words):

One could plausibly argue that intelligence is genuinely both innate and developed. The Minnesota Twin Study put IQ heritability at 50–70%, yet the Flynn Effect shows IQ rising 3 points per decade for nearly a century — clearly an environmental signal, since gene pools don't shift that fast. UNESCO (2022) likewise links early-childhood investment to measurable cognitive gains. What this implies is that genes set the range, while environment determines where you sit within it. Were policymakers to internalise this, they'd invest far more aggressively in early-years education and nutrition.
Q3. How will AI change education in the next 20 years?
P: AI is poised to transform education from a one-size-fits-all model into a deeply personalised ecosystem, though this transition will be neither smooth nor uncontested.

E: Generative AI's capacity for adaptive tutoring, instant feedback, and content generation dwarfs anything textbooks could ever offer, but it simultaneously threatens academic integrity and the very pedagogy of human mentorship.

E: A 2023 Stanford HAI report found that AI tutoring systems improved student outcomes by an average of 0.4 standard deviations — comparable to one-on-one human tutoring. UNESCO's 2023 guidance on generative AI flagged that by mid-2023, over half of teachers globally had encountered AI-generated submissions. 3. Predict 3 Ideas (Advanced)

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

Good afternoon. In today's session I'd like to examine a question that has, um, animated educational theorists since the advent of MOOCs around 2012 — namely, whether asynchronous digital learning genuinely delivers on its emancipatory promise, or whether it merely repackages old inequities in shinier wrapping. [pause]

Let's begin with the figure of the autodidact. Historically, self-taught learners — think of Benjamin Franklin or Frederick Douglass — were celebrated as proof that intellect would, given access to books, transcend social station. Platforms like Coursera and edX have, in theory, multiplied such opportunities a thousandfold. However, recent data is rather sobering: completion rates for free online courses hover stubbornly around seven per cent. [pause]

Now, why is this? Well, three factors warrant attention. Firstly, the absence of didactic scaffolding — by which I mean the deliberate sequencing and feedback that a skilled instructor provides — means that learners frequently plateau. Secondly, what linguists call fossilisation sets in: errors, once habituated, become extraordinarily difficult to dislodge without intervention. Thirdly, and perhaps most damningly, the meritocracy these platforms purport to enable assumes a level playing field that simply, frankly, doesn't exist. Learners from lower socioeconomic backgrounds lack the broadband, the quiet study space, and indeed the cultural capital to navigate university-grade content. [pause]

So what's the way forward? Reformers advocate a hybrid model — sometimes called holistic pedagogy — which marries the flexibility of asynchronous access with periodic synchronous tutorials. Early evidence from Scandinavia suggests retention rates triple under this arrangement. [pause]

Let me turn now to a piece of evidence that I find genuinely unsettling for the optimists in this field. A team at the University of Pennsylvania — Lou and Reich, if you want the citation — examined enrolment data from sixty-eight Coursera courses, and they found something they rather aptly nicknamed the "Matthew effect" of online learning. The phrase, of course, comes from the gospel: to those who have, more shall be given. In practice, this meant that learners who already held a bachelor's degree were not merely more likely to enrol, but vastly more likely to complete — and, crucially, to report a tangible career benefit. The platforms, in other words, were not flattening the educational hierarchy; they were, um, quietly steepening it. [pause]

What complicates this picture is a subtlety about motivation. Now, you might assume that those seven per cent who finish are simply more disciplined. But qualitative interviews suggest something more structural: completers tend to have what sociologists call "warm handovers" — a mentor, a workplace, a family member who validates the effort. The isolated autodidact, hunched over a laptop at midnight with no such scaffolding, tends to drift. Self-direction, it turns out, is far less an individual virtue than a socially distributed resource. [pause]

A further consideration, and one the techno-utopians rarely concede, is credentialism. Even a flawlessly completed MOOC certificate carries, well, negligible signalling value in most labour markets. Employers still privilege the brand of the bricks-and-mortar institution. So the autodidact may genuinely master econometrics or Python, yet remain locked out by a gatekeeping mechanism that has nothing to do with competence and everything to do with prestige. [pause]

The blended Scandinavian model I mentioned earlier addresses the pedagogical gap — but it does nothing, frankly, about this credentialing wall. And that, if you like, is where the conversation must shift from pedagogy to policy — let me flag the key policy implication…

Before we close, one caveat: we mustn't romanticise traditional classrooms either. The rote-learning culture that still dominates much of secondary schooling globally suppresses, rather than fosters, the very curiosity that drives genuine autodidacts.

The diagram outlines the seven-stage postgraduate admission process at a leading university, from initial application to final enrolment.

Overall, the procedure begins with online submission and culminates in either acceptance into the enrolment cohort or formal rejection, with several peer-reviewed checkpoints in between. The pathway is clearly conditional, since a substantial proportion of candidates are filtered out at the early stages.

At the outset, the application is submitted online by the candidate and is subsequently screened by the admissions office for basic eligibility, including credentials and language proficiency. Once this preliminary stage has been completed, eligible files are forwarded to the relevant faculty, where academic credentials, statements of purpose and references are carefully evaluated.

Shortlisted applicants are then invited to a panel interview, and doctoral candidates must additionally submit a research proposal for peer review before the panel scores are collated. Should the candidate satisfy the panel's criteria, an offer is relayed by email, after which a deposit confirms placement in the enrolment cohort. Unsuccessful applicants receive written feedback and may reapply in the following cycle, returning the process to its starting point.

The flow chart delineates the seven discrete stages through which a postgraduate application progresses at a leading institution, from online submission to eventual enrolment or rejection.

Overall, what the diagram reveals is an emphatically conditional pathway: at successive checkpoints, candidates are either advanced or eliminated, so that only those satisfying each criterion reach the final decision. The procedure is also recursive, since rejected applicants may re-enter the cycle.

The sequence is initiated when the application is submitted online, whereupon it undergoes eligibility screening by the admissions office. Upon completion of this preliminary check, eligible files are forwarded to the relevant faculty, where statements of purpose and references are appraised.

Thereafter, shortlisted applicants are summoned to a panel interview, while doctoral candidates are additionally required to submit a research proposal for peer review before scores are collated. Were a candidate to meet the panel's threshold, an offer would be relayed by email, with a deposit securing the enrolment cohort placement. Those rejected, by contrast, are issued a feedback letter and may re-apply in the subsequent cycle.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~270 words)

Whether university education should be made free or continue to require tuition fees is a controversial issue in many countries. This essay will examine both sides of the argument before suggesting that a means-tested system represents the most defensible compromise.

Supporters of tuition-free universities argue that exorbitant fees deter capable students from low-income households, thereby undermining a genuine meritocracy. Countries such as Germany, for example, have abolished tuition for domestic students and still maintain a rigorous academic standard. It is this kind of model that arguably maximises human capital, since no talented young person is excluded from tertiary education simply because of their financial background. Moreover, removing fees could ease the student-debt crisis, which currently delays many graduates from buying houses or starting families.

On the other side, critics contend that providing free higher education places a heavy burden on taxpayers, many of whom never benefit from a degree themselves. There is also a concern that, without the financial commitment of tuition fees, students may take their studies less seriously, leading to higher rates of truancy and procrastination. Furthermore, an unrestricted intake might cause degree devaluation, since employers struggle to distinguish candidates when nearly everyone holds a bachelor's qualification.

In my opinion, neither extreme is fully satisfactory, and the most workable solution lies somewhere in between. Tuition should be heavily subsidised but not entirely waived; students from disadvantaged families ought to receive needs-based scholarships, while those who can comfortably afford fees should contribute. Such a system protects equity without bankrupting the public purse, and a modest contribution would encourage the academic discipline that fully free systems sometimes struggle to maintain.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~295 words)

Whether tertiary education ought to be publicly financed or remain fee-based is a debate that cuts to the heart of contemporary educational policy. While both positions have considerable merit, I shall argue that a calibrated, means-tested model — rather than universal tuition or wholesale gratuity — best reconciles the competing imperatives of access, efficiency and fiscal sustainability.

Advocates of free university maintain that exorbitant tuition entrenches socio-economic stratification. Cross-national data appear to support this: Germany and several Nordic states, having abolished domestic fees, report relatively high participation rates among first-generation students. It is precisely this widening of the educational pipeline that proponents regard as essential to a functioning meritocracy. Were tuition entirely removed, moreover, the chilling effect of debt on consumption and family formation — particularly acute in the United States, where outstanding student liabilities exceed USD 1.7 trillion — would arguably be mitigated.

Opponents, by contrast, contend that universal gratuity is fiscally regressive. Public funds, drawn disproportionately from non-graduate taxpayers, are channelled toward future high earners, a transfer difficult to justify on equity grounds. Not only does indiscriminate provision risk degree devaluation, but it may also weaken academic commitment, since tuition, however modest, often functions as a commitment device against procrastination. By the same token, blanket subsidies tend to crowd out investment in the vocational pathways the labour market increasingly demands.

The position I would advocate, accordingly, is a tiered model contingent upon household income: full subsidy for the lowest quintile, sliding contributions for the middle, and means-tested loans for the affluent. Such an architecture preserves the egalitarian ethos of free access while inoculating the system against the moral hazard and fiscal drift that critics rightly identify. Notwithstanding the political difficulty of implementation, it is calibration — not abolition — that should guide reform.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc phức cao cấp xuyên suốt (cleft 'It is precisely this widening... that', đảo ngữ điều kiện 'Were tuition entirely removed', đảo ngữ phủ định 'Not only does... but also') trong khi Band 7 chỉ có một cleft.

•  Band 8 lexis chính sách dày đặc ('fiscally regressive', 'commitment device', 'blanket subsidies', 'egalitarian ethos', 'moral hazard', 'fiscal drift', 'gratuity') và cohesion ngầm theo dòng chủ đề, vượt Band 7 vốn còn dùng linker máy móc.

> **Rote learning** often hinders genuine comprehension and suppresses creativity in the classroom.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'rote' nghe giống 'robot' → học như robot, lặp đi lặp lại không suy nghĩ.
vocabulary.common_error: Không dùng *rote learn* như động từ; nói *learn by rote* hoặc dùng danh từ *rote learning*.
vocabulary.definition_en: learning by mechanical repetition and memorisation, often without genuine understanding of the material
vocabulary.definition_vi: học vẹt (học thuộc lòng máy móc, không hiểu bản chất)
vocabulary.example: Rote learning often hinders genuine comprehension and suppresses creativity in the classroom.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'rote' nghe giống 'robot' → học như robot, lặp đi lặp lại không suy nghĩ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Giáo dục bậc đại học hoặc cao đẳng, sau bậc trung học.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Tertiary education** is seldom affordable for families in rural areas.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
tertiary giống 'third' (thứ ba) trong hệ thống giáo dục: primary → secondary → tertiary.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Tertiary' (bậc ba, sau secondary) khác 'primary' và 'secondary'; đừng nhầm với 'territory'.
vocabulary.definition_en: education at college or university level, following secondary schooling
vocabulary.definition_vi: giáo dục bậc đại học/cao đẳng (sau trung học)
vocabulary.example: Tertiary education is seldom affordable for families in rural areas.
vocabulary.memory_hook: tertiary giống 'third' (thứ ba) trong hệ thống giáo dục: primary → secondary → tertiary.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Người tự học, tự trau dồi kiến thức mà không qua đào tạo chính quy.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Were the world's great **autodidacts** judged solely by their credentials, history would have overlooked them entirely.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
auto- (tự) + didact (dạy, như 'didactic') → người tự dạy chính mình.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'autodidact' (danh từ chỉ người) với 'didactic' (tính từ, mang tính giáo huấn).
vocabulary.definition_en: a person who has taught themselves a subject or skill without formal instruction
vocabulary.definition_vi: người tự học (tự trau dồi kiến thức mà không qua đào tạo chính quy)
vocabulary.example: Were the world's great autodidacts judged solely by their credentials, history would have overlooked them entirely.
vocabulary.memory_hook: auto- (tự) + didact (dạy, như 'didactic') → người tự dạy chính mình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đạo văn, sao chép ý tưởng hoặc lời văn của người khác mà không trích dẫn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A student should under no circumstances commit **plagiarism**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
liên tưởng 'plagiarism' với 'copy-paste không xin phép' → đạo văn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Plagiarism' là danh từ không đếm được; động từ tương ứng là 'plagiarise' (Anh) / 'plagiarize' (Mỹ).
vocabulary.definition_en: the act of presenting another person's words or ideas as one's own without acknowledgement
vocabulary.definition_vi: đạo văn (sao chép ý tưởng/lời văn của người khác mà không trích dẫn)
vocabulary.example: A student should under no circumstances commit plagiarism.
vocabulary.memory_hook: liên tưởng 'plagiarism' với 'copy-paste không xin phép' → đạo văn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự trốn học, thường xuyên nghỉ học không phép.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We will on no account tolerate **truancy** in this school.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
truant nghe gần 'true-ant' nhưng nghĩa là kẻ trốn học → truancy là hành vi đó.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Truancy' là danh từ trừu tượng; người trốn học gọi là 'a truant', không phải 'a truancy'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the habitual practice of staying away from school without leave or explanation
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự trốn học (thường xuyên nghỉ học không phép)
vocabulary.example: We will on no account tolerate truancy in this school.
vocabulary.memory_hook: truant nghe gần 'true-ant' nhưng nghĩa là kẻ trốn học → truancy là hành vi đó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Toàn diện, xem xét sự phát triển tổng thể chứ không tách rời từng mặt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Schools ought to nurture students' **holistic** development, not just their academic results.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
holistic chứa 'whole' (toàn bộ) về mặt âm và nghĩa → nhìn nhận toàn diện.
vocabulary.common_error: Không dùng *holistic* với nghĩa đơn thuần là “nhiều”; từ này nhấn mạnh việc xem xét các phần như một tổng thể.
vocabulary.definition_en: dealing with or considering something as a whole rather than in separate parts, especially in relation to a person's overall development
vocabulary.definition_vi: toàn diện (xem xét tổng thể, không tách rời từng phần)
vocabulary.example: Schools ought to nurture students' holistic development, not just their academic results.
vocabulary.memory_hook: holistic chứa 'whole' (toàn bộ) về mặt âm và nghĩa → nhìn nhận toàn diện.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá cao, cắt cổ — thường dùng để mô tả học phí hoặc giá cả bất hợp lý.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> So **exorbitant** have tuition fees become that the prospect of tertiary education is, for many working-class families, a financial pipe dream.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
ex- (vượt ra ngoài) + orbit (quỹ đạo) → giá cả 'vượt quỹ đạo bình thường' → quá cao.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Exorbitant' chỉ dùng cho giá cả/chi phí/yêu cầu, không dùng để mô tả kích thước vật lý.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a price, fee, or demand) unreasonably high; far exceeding what is normal or acceptable
vocabulary.definition_vi: quá cao, cắt cổ (về giá cả, học phí)
vocabulary.example: So exorbitant have tuition fees become that the prospect of tertiary education is, for many working-class families, a financial pipe dream.
vocabulary.memory_hook: ex- (vượt ra ngoài) + orbit (quỹ đạo) → giá cả 'vượt quỹ đạo bình thường' → quá cao.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phương pháp sư phạm, cách thức và lý luận về việc giảng dạy.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> What contemporary **pedagogy** increasingly champions is a holistic framework, one privileging emotional intelligence over narrow academic metrics.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
ped- (trẻ em, như 'pediatric') + -agogy (dẫn dắt) → khoa học dẫn dắt việc học.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong tiếng Anh-Anh, đuôi '-gogy' phát âm là /-dʒi/, không phát âm nặng như 'ped-a-GOG-ee' kiểu Mỹ.
vocabulary.definition_en: the method and practice of teaching, especially as an academic subject or theoretical concept
vocabulary.definition_vi: phương pháp sư phạm, khoa học giảng dạy
vocabulary.example: What contemporary pedagogy increasingly champions is a holistic framework, one privileging emotional intelligence over narrow academic metrics.
vocabulary.memory_hook: ped- (trẻ em, như 'pediatric') + -agogy (dẫn dắt) → khoa học dẫn dắt việc học.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chương trình học, giáo trình của một khóa học hay bậc học.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> An over-reliance on standardised testing narrows the **curriculum** into a teach-to-the-test straitjacket.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
curriculum gần với 'career' + 'run' (a course one runs through) → lộ trình học tập.
vocabulary.common_error: Số nhiều của 'curriculum' có thể là 'curricula' (học thuật) hoặc 'curriculums'; tránh viết 'curriculums' trong văn phong academic.
vocabulary.definition_en: the subjects comprising a course of study in a school or college, and the way they are structured
vocabulary.definition_vi: chương trình học, giáo trình
vocabulary.example: An over-reliance on standardised testing narrows the curriculum into a teach-to-the-test straitjacket.
vocabulary.memory_hook: curriculum gần với 'career' + 'run' (a course one runs through) → lộ trình học tập.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuộc về hướng nghiệp, đào tạo kỹ năng nghề cụ thể.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> There is a compelling case for rebalancing higher education towards **vocational** pathways, particularly in economies plagued by graduate underemployment.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
vocation (nghề nghiệp, thiên hướng) + -al → liên quan đến nghề nghiệp, dạy nghề.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm *vocational* (thuộc đào tạo nghề) với *vacational*; thường đi với *training, education, qualification*.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to an occupation or employment, especially education or training directed at a particular skill or trade
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuộc về hướng nghiệp, dạy nghề
vocabulary.example: There is a compelling case for rebalancing higher education towards vocational pathways, particularly in economies plagued by graduate underemployment.
vocabulary.memory_hook: vocation (nghề nghiệp, thiên hướng) + -al → liên quan đến nghề nghiệp, dạy nghề.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Năng khiếu, khả năng bẩm sinh cho một lĩnh vực nào đó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> She showed a natural **aptitude** for languages from a very young age.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
aptitude gần với 'apt' (phù hợp, có khả năng) → khả năng tự nhiên phù hợp với việc gì đó.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Aptitude' (năng khiếu bẩm sinh) khác 'attitude' (thái độ) — hai từ dễ viết nhầm vì gần giống mặt chữ.
vocabulary.definition_en: a natural ability or talent for learning or doing a particular thing
vocabulary.definition_vi: năng khiếu, khả năng bẩm sinh
vocabulary.example: She showed a natural aptitude for languages from a very young age.
vocabulary.memory_hook: aptitude gần với 'apt' (phù hợp, có khả năng) → khả năng tự nhiên phù hợp với việc gì đó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Không đồng bộ — việc học diễn ra không cùng thời điểm với giảng viên hay lớp học.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The lecturer examined whether **asynchronous** digital learning genuinely delivers on its emancipatory promise, or merely repackages old inequities.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
a- (không) + synchronous (đồng bộ, như 'synchronise') → không cùng lúc.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Asynchronous' mô tả việc học không diễn ra cùng lúc; đối lập trực tiếp là 'synchronous' (đồng bộ, trực tiếp cùng thời điểm), không phải 'offline'.
vocabulary.definition_en: not occurring or existing at the same time; in learning, referring to study that does not require real-time interaction with an instructor
vocabulary.definition_vi: không đồng bộ (học không cần diễn ra cùng thời điểm với giảng viên)
vocabulary.example: The lecturer examined whether asynchronous digital learning genuinely delivers on its emancipatory promise, or merely repackages old inequities.
vocabulary.memory_hook: a- (không) + synchronous (đồng bộ, như 'synchronise') → không cùng lúc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ngoại khóa, chỉ các hoạt động nằm ngoài chương trình học chính khóa.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Students rarely have time for **extracurricular** activities during exam season.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
extra- (ngoài) + curricular (thuộc chương trình học) → ngoài chương trình học chính khóa.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết liền *extracurricular*; thường dùng trước danh từ như *activities*, không nói *an extracurricular* nếu thiếu danh từ ngữ cảnh.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to activities outside the regular school or college curriculum
vocabulary.definition_vi: ngoại khóa (hoạt động ngoài chương trình học chính khóa)
vocabulary.example: Students rarely have time for extracurricular activities during exam season.
vocabulary.memory_hook: extra- (ngoài) + curricular (thuộc chương trình học) → ngoài chương trình học chính khóa.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nghiêm ngặt, khắt khe — thường mô tả tiêu chuẩn học thuật cao.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I have never seen such a **rigorous** curriculum in my life.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
rigorous nghe giống 'rigid' (cứng nhắc) → tiêu chuẩn khắt khe, không dễ dãi.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm *rigorous* (nghiêm ngặt, kỹ lưỡng) với *vigorous* (mạnh mẽ, đầy năng lượng).
vocabulary.definition_en: thorough, exhaustive, and demanding strict precision or high standards
vocabulary.definition_vi: nghiêm ngặt, khắt khe (về tiêu chuẩn học thuật)
vocabulary.example: I have never seen such a rigorous curriculum in my life.
vocabulary.memory_hook: rigorous nghe giống 'rigid' (cứng nhắc) → tiêu chuẩn khắt khe, không dễ dãi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vốn con người — kiến thức và kỹ năng của người lao động xét theo giá trị kinh tế.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Public funding of universities is often framed as an investment in **human capital**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
capital (vốn) thường nghĩ đến tiền, nhưng 'human capital' là 'vốn' nằm trong con người: kỹ năng, kiến thức.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Human capital' là thuật ngữ kinh tế học, không viết hoa và không dùng số nhiều ('human capitals' là sai).
vocabulary.definition_en: the skills, knowledge, and experience possessed by individuals or a population, viewed in terms of their economic value
vocabulary.definition_vi: vốn con người (kiến thức, kỹ năng của người lao động xét về giá trị kinh tế)
vocabulary.example: Public funding of universities is often framed as an investment in human capital.
vocabulary.memory_hook: capital (vốn) thường nghĩ đến tiền, nhưng 'human capital' là 'vốn' nằm trong con người: kỹ năng, kiến thức.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thức khuya để học bài hoặc hoàn thành công việc quan trọng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I have a big exam tomorrow, so I need to **burn the midnight oil** tonight.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ngày xưa người ta đốt dầu đèn (oil lamp) để có ánh sáng học/làm việc ban đêm → thức khuya.
collocations: burn the midnight oil before exams
burn the midnight oil to finish a project
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là thành ngữ cố định; không đổi thành *burn midnight oil* và không dùng trong văn học thuật quá trang trọng.
vocabulary.definition_en: to study or work late into the night, especially to prepare for something important
vocabulary.definition_vi: thức khuya học bài/làm việc
vocabulary.example: I have a big exam tomorrow, so I need to burn the midnight oil tonight.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Ngày xưa người ta đốt dầu đèn (oil lamp) để có ánh sáng học/làm việc ban đêm → thức khuya.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vượt qua một kỳ thi hoặc thử thách một cách xuất sắc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> She studied extremely hard and **passed the final exam with flying colours**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Flying colours' vốn là lá cờ chiến thắng tung bay trên tàu chiến trở về → thắng lợi vẻ vang.
collocations: pass an exam with flying colours
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *pass an exam with flying colours*; không nói *get flying colours* và lưu ý chính tả Anh-Anh *colours*.
vocabulary.definition_en: to succeed in a test or examination with an excellent result
vocabulary.definition_vi: vượt qua (kỳ thi) một cách xuất sắc
vocabulary.example: She studied extremely hard and passed the final exam with flying colours.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Flying colours' vốn là lá cờ chiến thắng tung bay trên tàu chiến trở về → thắng lợi vẻ vang.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Học sinh được giáo viên yêu thích, ưu ái hơn các bạn khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He was teased by his classmates for being the **teacher's pet**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
pet (thú cưng) → 'teacher's pet' là học trò được giáo viên 'cưng chiều' như thú cưng.
collocations: be teased for being the teacher's pet
vocabulary.common_error: Cần sở hữu cách *teacher’s pet*; sắc thái thường châm biếm/tiêu cực, không phải lời khen trung tính.
vocabulary.definition_en: a pupil who is, or is seen to be, favoured by the teacher over the other pupils
vocabulary.definition_vi: học sinh cưng của giáo viên
vocabulary.example: He was teased by his classmates for being the teacher's pet.
vocabulary.memory_hook: pet (thú cưng) → 'teacher's pet' là học trò được giáo viên 'cưng chiều' như thú cưng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bắt tay vào học hành một cách chăm chỉ, nghiêm túc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It would be a chance to **hit the books** with real purpose rather than merely scraping through.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
hit (đánh, lao vào) + books (sách) → 'lao vào sách vở' để học nghiêm túc.
collocations: have to hit the books tonight
vocabulary.common_error: *Hit the books* nghĩa là bắt đầu học nghiêm túc, không phải “đánh vào sách”; chỉ phù hợp văn nói/thân mật.
vocabulary.definition_en: to begin, or apply oneself to, studying
vocabulary.definition_vi: bắt tay vào học, học hành chăm chỉ
vocabulary.example: It would be a chance to hit the books with real purpose rather than merely scraping through.
vocabulary.memory_hook: hit (đánh, lao vào) + books (sách) → 'lao vào sách vở' để học nghiêm túc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vượt qua một kỳ thi hoặc tình huống khó khăn một cách chật vật, sát nút.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Since he prepared well, he managed to **scrape through** the test without any stress.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
scrape (cạo, cà sát) qua khe hẹp → vừa đủ lọt qua, suýt soát.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Scrape through' hàm ý vừa đủ đậu, sát nút; không dùng khi muốn diễn tả một kết quả xuất sắc.
vocabulary.definition_en: to narrowly succeed in passing a test, exam, or difficult situation
vocabulary.definition_vi: vượt qua một cách chật vật, suýt trượt
vocabulary.example: Since he prepared well, he managed to scrape through the test without any stress.
vocabulary.memory_hook: scrape (cạo, cà sát) qua khe hẹp → vừa đủ lọt qua, suýt soát.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mọt sách, người ham đọc sách và dành nhiều thời gian cho việc học/đọc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> She's a real **bookworm**; she spends all her weekends at the library reading.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
worm (con sâu) sống trong sách → hình ảnh 'con mọt sách' đục khoét, gặm nhấm sách suốt ngày.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết liền *bookworm*; dùng cho người đọc nhiều, không dùng để chỉ chính cuốn sách hay hành động đọc.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person who reads or studies a great deal, often to the exclusion of other activities
vocabulary.definition_vi: mọt sách (người ham đọc sách)
vocabulary.example: She's a real bookworm; she spends all her weekends at the library reading.
vocabulary.memory_hook: worm (con sâu) sống trong sách → hình ảnh 'con mọt sách' đục khoét, gặm nhấm sách suốt ngày.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiện tượng lỗi sai trở nên cố định, khó sửa trong quá trình học ngôn ngữ hoặc kỹ năng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> What linguists call **fossilisation** sets in: errors, once habituated, become extraordinarily difficult to dislodge without intervention.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
fossil (hóa thạch) → lỗi sai 'hóa thạch', cứng đờ, không thể sửa được nữa.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Fossilisation' trong ngôn ngữ học chỉ lỗi bị 'đóng băng' vĩnh viễn, khác với nghĩa gốc 'hóa thạch' trong địa chất học.
vocabulary.definition_en: in language or skill learning, the permanent settling of incorrect forms or habits that become highly resistant to correction
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự hóa thạch lỗi sai (lỗi trở nên cố định, khó sửa trong quá trình học)
vocabulary.example: What linguists call fossilisation sets in: errors, once habituated, become extraordinarily difficult to dislodge without intervention.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sân chơi bình đẳng, tình huống mọi người có cơ hội thành công ngang nhau.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The meritocracy these platforms purport to enable assumes a **level playing field** that simply doesn't exist.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Sân bóng (playing field) phải bằng phẳng (level) để hai đội thi đấu công bằng → cơ hội ngang nhau cho mọi người.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường dùng *a level playing field*; không bỏ mạo từ khi nói về một tình huống công bằng cụ thể.
vocabulary.definition_en: a situation in which everyone has an equal chance of succeeding, without unfair advantages or disadvantages
vocabulary.definition_vi: sân chơi bình đẳng (cơ hội công bằng cho tất cả)
